draft.title: Homelessness and public housing
card: Homelessness means a person has no suitable place to live. It includes sleeping rough, staying in crisis accommodation, couch surfing and living in overcrowded housing.
homes owned and managed by a state government and rented to people on low incomes, usually at a rent set as a share of the tenant's income.
a wider term. It covers public housing and also homes run by community housing providers, which are not-for-profit organisations.
Demand is greater than supply, so waiting lists are long and many people wait for years. Homelessness has been rising, and it shows that housing support does not reach everyone who needs it.
draft.remember: Governments supply public and social housing for people on low incomes, but supply falls short of need.

a.q: Which of these is an example of social housing that is not public housing?
opts: A home run by a not-for-profit community housing provider
A home bought by a family with a mortgage
A flat rented from a private landlord at market rent
A unit in a strata scheme owned by its occupant
a.why: Social housing includes homes run by community housing providers, not only those run by a state government. A privately rented flat is not social housing, because the landlord is a private owner who charges market rent.
a.clue: Think about who owns and runs the home, and why.

b.q: Jess is on a low income in Newcastle and has waited four years for a public housing home. What does her situation best show?
opts: Demand for public housing is greater than the supply
Public housing is not meant for people on low incomes
The law gives every person a right to a public home
Community housing providers cannot rent to low earners
b.why: A wait of years for a home shows that there are more eligible people than homes. The law does not give a right to housing in Australia, so the wait does not mean a right has been breached. That is why the third option is wrong, even though it may seem to fit.
b.clue: Ask what a long wait says about homes compared with people needing them.

a.best: A home run by a not-for-profit community housing provider

b.best: Demand for public housing is greater than the supply

problems.detail: The ABS definition of homelessness covers people in 'severely crowded' dwellings, not anyone in 'overcrowded housing'. Ordinary crowding is not counted as homelessness, so the card overstates the definition.
The clue ('what a long wait says about homes compared with people needing them') nearly states the answer, so students can pick 'demand is greater than supply' without applying the idea.
Why (b) rules out the third option because there is no legal right to housing in Australia. That idea belongs to point 1 and is not taught on this card.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer. The card loosely says 'overcrowded' where the ABS definition says 'severely crowded', the clue for b gives the answer away, and why (b) leans on the right-to-housing idea from point 1.

proposal.title: Homelessness and public housing
card: Homelessness means a person has no suitable place to live. The Australian Bureau of Statistics counts people sleeping rough, in crisis accommodation, couch surfing with others, and in severely crowded dwellings.
homes owned and managed by a state government and rented to people on low incomes, usually at a rent set as a share of the tenant's income.
a wider term for housing for people on low incomes. It covers public housing and also homes run by community housing providers, which are not-for-profit organisations.
Demand is greater than supply, so waiting lists are long and many people wait for years. Homelessness has been rising, and it shows that housing support does not reach everyone who needs it.
proposal.remember: Governments supply public and social housing for people on low incomes, but supply falls short of need.

opts: A home run by a not-for-profit community housing provider
A home bought by a family with a mortgage

A unit in a strata scheme owned by its occupant
a.why: Social housing includes homes run by community housing providers, not only those run by a state government. A privately rented flat is not social housing, because the landlord is a private owner who charges market rent.
a.clue: Think about who owns and runs the home, and why.

b.q: Jess is on a low income in Newcastle and has waited four years for a public housing home. What does her situation best show?
opts: Demand for public housing is greater than the supply
Supply of public housing is greater than the demand
Public housing is not meant for people on low incomes
Community housing providers cannot rent to low earners
b.why: Jess is on a low income, so she is the kind of person public housing is for. A wait of years means there are more eligible people than homes. If supply were greater than demand, eligible people would be housed quickly, so the reversed option is wrong.
b.clue: Is Jess eligible, and if so, why is she still waiting?
